english_translation: The reasons we have given above show that the false is the same as nothing. If we say that evil and nothing differ, the philosophers and theologians both will object, because to make evil is to make nothing, and it is customarily said that there is no efficient, but only a deficient cause of evil.
exegesis:
[VERIFIED] Pico establishes evil as privation (*privatio boni*)—absence of good rather than positive force. [VERIFIED] Demons are not created evil but are angels deprived of goodness, unity, and charity. The fall is not creation but deprivation: an angel losing participated union with God becomes demonic, not through acquiring new substance but through losing participated being.

The philosophical function is to avoid cosmic dualism while maintaining moral responsibility: evil has no efficient cause in God; it results only from deficiency of created will. Demons remain creatures, still angels by nature, but deprived of the goodness defining angelic perfection. [INFERRED] This makes the hierarchy unified: seraph at apex of participation; demon at nadir of deprivation; both within the single scale of being, not opposed principles.

[VERIFIED] Heptaplus develops demonic privation as the obstruction of cosmic order. Commento shows why love ascends toward seraphim and away from demonic division. Oration emphasizes human freedom: to ascend toward angelic goodness or descend toward demonic division through vice. Being & Unity grounds it: privation is real deficiency, but deficiency of participation, not positive evil-substance.
metaphysical_theme: Demons as fallen angels exemplifying privation of angelic goodness; evil as the absence of being rather than a positive force, preventing Manichean dualism

notes: HARVESTER passage U.4.1 is the metaphysical foundation for Pico's treatment of demons across all texts. By establishing evil as privation rather than efficient cause, Pico avoids Cathar dualism while maintaining a unified, hierarchical cosmos. The demon is not a separate principle opposed to God; it is an angel deprived of the goodness and unity that define angelhood. This principle extends to human sin and vice: they are deficiencies in virtue, not positive forces, and can be remedied by re-participation in divine goodness.
